data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a rational, non-inductive methodological decision to prefer the theory with the highest verisimilitude (truth-likeness) among surviving competitors, without asserting its probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be empirically estimated without relying on inductive assumptions about the representativeness of past tests.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severe test' implicitly requires the assumption that nature is uniform.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Verisimilitude-based selection: Corroboration reports past survival against severe tests. While this does not increase logical probability (which remains zero or low for universal laws), it provides the only available indicator that a theory has greater content and has withstood attempts to falsify it.
